19Math · Linear algebra

Vectors → matrices → determinant → Jacobian: what one “layer” actually computes.

ⓘ Notes
The linear algebra a neural network uses, with step-by-step proofs of the dot product’s geometry, the transpose rule, the area formula and the transpose rule for gradients.

Why it’s designed this way: These few rules are what you need to read the formulas for a layer and for attention.

MathWhere the model uses it
② Diagram

Inside a model a word is a Vectors & dot product; a layer is a Matrix multiplication; when Backprop sends gradients back, it multiplies by the transpose. This stop explains each and proves the key formulas step by step.

  • Vectors & dot product: how much two directions agree; an ① Score is a dot product.
  • Linear maps & determinant: how much a matrix stretches or squashes area.
  • Transpose & Jacobian: the derivative for many inputs and outputs, and why gradients get multiplied by the transpose.
③ Details · why

An nnn-dimensional vector is nnn numbers, a=(a1,…,an)a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)a=(a1​,…,an​). The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up, and the length (norm) is defined from it:

a⋅b=∑i=1naibi,∥a∥=a⋅aa\cdot b=\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i,\qquad \|a\|=\sqrt{a\cdot a}a⋅b=i=1∑n​ai​bi​,∥a∥=a⋅a​
a⋅b=∑i=1naibi∥a∥=a⋅a\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}a\cdot b&=\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}\|a\|&=\sqrt{a\cdot a}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}a⋅b​=i=1∑n​ai​bi​​∥a∥​=a⋅a​​​
a⋅b=∑i=1naibi∥a∥=a⋅a\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}&a\cdot b\\&\quad =\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}&\|a\|\\&\quad =\sqrt{a\cdot a}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}​a⋅b=i=1∑n​ai​bi​​​∥a∥=a⋅a​​​

It is symmetric, a⋅b=b⋅aa\cdot b=b\cdot aa⋅b=b⋅a, and bilinear, (a+c)⋅b=a⋅b+c⋅b(a+c)\cdot b=a\cdot b+c\cdot b(a+c)⋅b=a⋅b+c⋅b and (ta)⋅b=t (a⋅b)(ta)\cdot b=t\,(a\cdot b)(ta)⋅b=t(a⋅b); each follows entry by entry from the definition.

📝 Geometric meaning: a⋅b=∥a∥ ∥b∥cos⁡θa\cdot b=\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\thetaa⋅b=∥a∥∥b∥cosθ (in 2-D and 3-D)

  1. Draw aaa and bbb from the same point; the third side of the triangle is a−ba-ba−b, and the angle between them is θ\thetaθ.
    Why: The three sides of a triangle.
  2. ∥a−b∥2=∥a∥2+∥b∥2−2∥a∥ ∥b∥cos⁡θ\|a-b\|^2=\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2-2\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\theta∥a−b∥2=∥a∥2+∥b∥2−2∥a∥∥b∥cosθ
    ∥a−b∥2=∥a∥2+∥b∥2−2∥a∥ ∥b∥cos⁡θ\begin{aligned}\|a-b\|^2&=\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2-2\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\theta\end{aligned}∥a−b∥2​=∥a∥2+∥b∥2−2∥a∥∥b∥cosθ​
    ∥a−b∥2=∥a∥2+∥b∥2−2∥a∥ ∥b∥cos⁡θ\begin{aligned}&\|a-b\|^2\\&\quad =\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2\\&\qquad -2\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\theta\end{aligned}​∥a−b∥2=∥a∥2+∥b∥2−2∥a∥∥b∥cosθ​
    Why: Law of cosines.
  3. ∥a−b∥2=(a−b)⋅(a−b)=∥a∥2−2 a⋅b+∥b∥2\|a-b\|^2=(a-b)\cdot(a-b)=\|a\|^2-2\,a\cdot b+\|b\|^2∥a−b∥2=(a−b)⋅(a−b)=∥a∥2−2a⋅b+∥b∥2
    ∥a−b∥2=(a−b)⋅(a−b)=∥a∥2−2 a⋅b+∥b∥2\begin{aligned}\|a-b\|^2&=(a-b)\cdot(a-b)\\&=\|a\|^2-2\,a\cdot b+\|b\|^2\end{aligned}∥a−b∥2​=(a−b)⋅(a−b)=∥a∥2−2a⋅b+∥b∥2​
    ∥a−b∥2=(a−b)⋅(a−b)=∥a∥2−2 a⋅b+∥b∥2\begin{aligned}&\|a-b\|^2\\&\quad =(a-b)\cdot(a-b)\\&\quad =\|a\|^2\\&\qquad -2\,a\cdot b+\|b\|^2\end{aligned}​∥a−b∥2=(a−b)⋅(a−b)=∥a∥2−2a⋅b+∥b∥2​
    Why: Definition of the norm, expanded with bilinearity and symmetry.
  4. a⋅b=∥a∥ ∥b∥cos⁡θa\cdot b=\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\thetaa⋅b=∥a∥∥b∥cosθ
    a⋅b=∥a∥ ∥b∥cos⁡θ\begin{aligned}a\cdot b&=\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\theta\end{aligned}a⋅b​=∥a∥∥b∥cosθ​
    a⋅b=∥a∥ ∥b∥cos⁡θ\begin{aligned}&a\cdot b\\&\quad =\|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\theta\end{aligned}​a⋅b=∥a∥∥b∥cosθ​
    Why: The right-hand sides are equal; cancel the common terms and divide by −2.

Q.E.D. ∎

In higher dimensions this is turned around and cos⁡θ=a⋅b∥a∥∥b∥\cos\theta=\frac{a\cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}cosθ=∥a∥∥b∥a⋅b​ defines the angle (the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality keeps it between −1 and 1; proof in the Optimization stop). This is “cosine similarity”: the more two word vectors point the same way, the closer it is to 1.

③ Details · why

An m×nm\times nm×n matrix AAA times an n×pn\times pn×p matrix BBB gives an m×pm\times pm×p matrix whose row iii, column jjj entry is the dot product of row iii of AAA with column jjj of BBB:

(AB)ij=∑k=1nAikBkj(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik}B_{kj}(AB)ij​=k=1∑n​Aik​Bkj​
(AB)ij=∑k=1nAikBkj\begin{aligned}(AB)_{ij}&=\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik}B_{kj}\end{aligned}(AB)ij​​=k=1∑n​Aik​Bkj​​
(AB)ij=∑k=1nAikBkj\begin{aligned}&(AB)_{ij}\\&\quad =\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_{ik}B_{kj}\end{aligned}​(AB)ij​=k=1∑n​Aik​Bkj​​

That is mpmpmp dot products of nnn multiplications each, mnpmnpmnp multiply-adds in total, which is where most of a large model’s compute goes. A fully connected layer y=Wx+by=Wx+by=Wx+b is a matrix times a vector; Q table (makes query cards) turns each word vector into a query; the attention score matrix is

S=QKTdk,Sij=qi⋅kjdkS=\frac{QK^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad S_{ij}=\frac{q_i\cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}S=dk​​QKT​,Sij​=dk​​qi​⋅kj​​
S=QKTdkSij=qi⋅kjdk\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}S&=\frac{QK^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}S_{ij}&=\frac{q_i\cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}S​=dk​​QKT​​Sij​​=dk​​qi​⋅kj​​​​
S=QKTdkSij=qi⋅kjdk\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}&S\\&\quad =\frac{QK^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}&S_{ij}\\&\quad =\frac{q_i\cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}​S=dk​​QKT​​​Sij​=dk​​qi​⋅kj​​​​

Matrix multiplication does not commute in general, AB≠BAAB\neq BAAB=BA. For example

(0100)(0010)=(1000),(0010)(0100)=(0001)\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}(00​10​)(01​00​)=(10​00​),(01​00​)(00​10​)=(00​01​)
(0100)(0010)=(1000)(0010)(0100)=(0001)\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}&=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}&=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}(00​10​)(01​00​)​=(10​00​)​(01​00​)(00​10​)​=(00​01​)​​
(0100)(0010)=(1000)(0010)(0100)=(0001)\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}&\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad =\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}&\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad =\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}​(00​10​)(01​00​)=(10​00​)​​(01​00​)(00​10​)=(00​01​)​​

📝 Transpose of a product: (AB)T=BTAT(AB)^{\mathsf T}=B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}(AB)T=BTAT

  1. ((AB)T)ij=(AB)ji\big((AB)^{\mathsf T}\big)_{ij}=(AB)_{ji}((AB)T)ij​=(AB)ji​
    ((AB)T)ij=(AB)ji\begin{aligned}\big((AB)^{\mathsf T}\big)_{ij}&=(AB)_{ji}\end{aligned}((AB)T)ij​​=(AB)ji​​
    ((AB)T)ij=(AB)ji\begin{aligned}&\big((AB)^{\mathsf T}\big)_{ij}\\&\quad =(AB)_{ji}\end{aligned}​((AB)T)ij​=(AB)ji​​
    Why: Definition of the transpose, (XT)ij=Xji(X^{\mathsf T})_{ij}=X_{ji}(XT)ij​=Xji​.
  2. (AB)ji=∑kAjkBki(AB)_{ji}=\sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki}(AB)ji​=k∑​Ajk​Bki​
    (AB)ji=∑kAjkBki\begin{aligned}(AB)_{ji}&=\sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki}\end{aligned}(AB)ji​​=k∑​Ajk​Bki​​
    (AB)ji=∑kAjkBki\begin{aligned}&(AB)_{ji}\\&\quad =\sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki}\end{aligned}​(AB)ji​=k∑​Ajk​Bki​​
    Why: Definition of the matrix product.
  3. ∑kAjkBki=∑k(BT)ik(AT)kj=(BTAT)ij\sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki}=\sum_k (B^{\mathsf T})_{ik}(A^{\mathsf T})_{kj}=(B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T})_{ij}k∑​Ajk​Bki​=k∑​(BT)ik​(AT)kj​=(BTAT)ij​
    ∑kAjkBki=∑k(BT)ik(AT)kj=(BTAT)ij\begin{aligned}\sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki}&=\sum_k (B^{\mathsf T})_{ik}(A^{\mathsf T})_{kj}\\&=(B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T})_{ij}\end{aligned}k∑​Ajk​Bki​​=k∑​(BT)ik​(AT)kj​=(BTAT)ij​​
    ∑kAjkBki=∑k(BT)ik(AT)kj=(BTAT)ij\begin{aligned}&\sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki}\\&\quad =\sum_k (B^{\mathsf T})_{ik}(A^{\mathsf T})_{kj}\\&\quad =(B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T})_{ij}\end{aligned}​k∑​Ajk​Bki​=k∑​(BT)ik​(AT)kj​=(BTAT)ij​​
    Why: Multiplication of numbers commutes; rewrite with the definitions of transpose and product.
  4. Every entry agrees, so the matrices are equal.

Q.E.D. ∎

③ Details · why

A 2×2 matrix sends every point xxx of the plane to AxAxAx. Its two columns are where the unit vectors go, Ae1=(a,c)Ae_1=(a,c)Ae1​=(a,c) and Ae2=(b,d)Ae_2=(b,d)Ae2​=(b,d), so the unit square becomes the parallelogram with those columns as sides.

A=(abcd),det⁡A=ad−bcA=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det A=ad-bcA=(ac​bd​),detA=ad−bc
A=(abcd)det⁡A=ad−bc\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}A&=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}\det A&=ad-bc\end{aligned}\end{gathered}A​=(ac​bd​)​detA​=ad−bc​​
A=(abcd)det⁡A=ad−bc\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}&A\\&\quad =\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}&\det A\\&\quad =ad\\&\qquad -bc\end{aligned}\end{gathered}​A=(ac​bd​)​​detA=ad−bc​​

📝 Parallelogram area =∣det⁡A∣=|\det A|=∣detA∣

  1. Let the sides be u=(a,c)u=(a,c)u=(a,c) and v=(b,d)v=(b,d)v=(b,d) with angle θ∈[0,π]\theta\in[0,\pi]θ∈[0,π]. Area = base × height = ∥u∥ ∥v∥sin⁡θ\|u\|\,\|v\|\sin\theta∥u∥∥v∥sinθ.
    Why: The height is ∥v∥sin⁡θ\|v\|\sin\theta∥v∥sinθ, and sin⁡θ≥0\sin\theta\ge 0sinθ≥0.
  2. Area2=∥u∥2∥v∥2(1−cos⁡2θ)=∥u∥2∥v∥2−(u⋅v)2\text{Area}^2=\|u\|^2\|v\|^2(1-\cos^2\theta)=\|u\|^2\|v\|^2-(u\cdot v)^2Area2=∥u∥2∥v∥2(1−cos2θ)=∥u∥2∥v∥2−(u⋅v)2
    Area2=∥u∥2∥v∥2(1−cos⁡2θ)=∥u∥2∥v∥2−(u⋅v)2\begin{aligned}\text{Area}^2&=\|u\|^2\|v\|^2(1-\cos^2\theta)\\&=\|u\|^2\|v\|^2-(u\cdot v)^2\end{aligned}Area2​=∥u∥2∥v∥2(1−cos2θ)=∥u∥2∥v∥2−(u⋅v)2​
    Area2=∥u∥2∥v∥2(1−cos⁡2θ)=∥u∥2∥v∥2−(u⋅v)2\begin{aligned}&\text{Area}^2\\&\quad =\|u\|^2\|v\|^2(1-\cos^2\theta)\\&\quad =\|u\|^2\|v\|^2\\&\qquad -(u\cdot v)^2\end{aligned}​Area2=∥u∥2∥v∥2(1−cos2θ)=∥u∥2∥v∥2−(u⋅v)2​
    Why: sin⁡2=1−cos⁡2\sin^2=1-\cos^2sin2=1−cos2, then u⋅v=∥u∥∥v∥cos⁡θu\cdot v=\|u\|\|v\|\cos\thetau⋅v=∥u∥∥v∥cosθ from the previous card.
  3. =(a2+c2)(b2+d2)−(ab+cd)2=(a^2+c^2)(b^2+d^2)-(ab+cd)^2=(a2+c2)(b2+d2)−(ab+cd)2
    =(a2+c2)(b2+d2)−(ab+cd)2\begin{aligned}&=(a^2+c^2)(b^2+d^2)-(ab+cd)^2\end{aligned}​=(a2+c2)(b2+d2)−(ab+cd)2​
    =(a2+c2)(b2+d2)−(ab+cd)2\begin{aligned}&\\&\quad =(a^2+c^2)(b^2+d^2)\\&\qquad -(ab+cd)^2\end{aligned}​=(a2+c2)(b2+d2)−(ab+cd)2​
    Why: Substitute the entries.
  4. =a2b2+a2d2+b2c2+c2d2−a2b2−2abcd−c2d2=(ad−bc)2=a^2b^2+a^2d^2+b^2c^2+c^2d^2-a^2b^2-2abcd-c^2d^2=(ad-bc)^2=a2b2+a2d2+b2c2+c2d2−a2b2−2abcd−c2d2=(ad−bc)2
    =a2b2+a2d2+b2c2+c2d2−a2b2−2abcd−c2d2=(ad−bc)2\begin{aligned}&=a^2b^2+a^2d^2+b^2c^2+c^2d^2-a^2b^2-2abcd-c^2d^2\\&=(ad-bc)^2\end{aligned}​=a2b2+a2d2+b2c2+c2d2−a2b2−2abcd−c2d2=(ad−bc)2​
    =a2b2+a2d2+b2c2+c2d2−a2b2−2abcd−c2d2=(ad−bc)2\begin{aligned}&\\&\quad =a^2b^2+a^2d^2+b^2c^2+c^2d^2\\&\qquad -a^2b^2-2abcd-c^2d^2\\&\quad =(ad-bc)^2\end{aligned}​=a2b2+a2d2+b2c2+c2d2−a2b2−2abcd−c2d2=(ad−bc)2​
    Why: Expand and cancel.
  5. Area=∣ad−bc∣=∣det⁡A∣\text{Area}=|ad-bc|=|\det A|Area=∣ad−bc∣=∣detA∣
    Area=∣ad−bc∣=∣det⁡A∣\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=|ad-bc|\\&=|\det A|\end{aligned}Area​=∣ad−bc∣=∣detA∣​
    Area=∣ad−bc∣=∣det⁡A∣\begin{aligned}&\text{Area}\\&\quad =|ad\\&\qquad -bc|\\&\quad =|\det A|\end{aligned}​Area=∣ad−bc∣=∣detA∣​
    Why: Area is non-negative; take square roots.

Q.E.D. ∎

The sign records orientation: det⁡A<0\det A<0detA<0 means the shape was flipped. When det⁡A=0\det A=0detA=0 the plane is squashed onto a line (or a point), different inputs land on the same output, information is lost, and the matrix has no inverse.

🧪 LabIllustrative

🧪 Drag a 2×2 matrix and watch the unit square

ⓘ You set the four entries; area and determinant are computed exactly.

Why it’s built this way:
  • The determinant’s formula is abstract; watching the square stretch, flip and collapse makes it stick.
👀 Try this:
  • Set b = c = 0: the square is stretched a times across and d times up, area = ad.
  • Set a = 1, b = 2, c = 0.5, d = 1: the determinant is 0 and the parallelogram collapses onto a line.
  • Swap the columns (a↔b, c↔d): the area stays, the determinant changes sign, the shape flips.
③ Details · why

When y=f(x)y=f(x)y=f(x) has nnn inputs and mmm outputs, its derivative is an m×nm\times nm×n matrix, the Jacobian:

Jij=∂yi∂xjJ_{ij}=\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}Jij​=∂xj​∂yi​​
Jij=∂yi∂xj\begin{aligned}J_{ij}&=\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}\end{aligned}Jij​​=∂xj​∂yi​​​
Jij=∂yi∂xj\begin{aligned}&J_{ij}\\&\quad =\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}\end{aligned}​Jij​=∂xj​∂yi​​​

📝 Gradient of a scalar loss LLL: ∇xL=JT ∇yL\nabla_x L=J^{\mathsf T}\,\nabla_y L∇x​L=JT∇y​L

  1. ∂L∂xj=∑i=1m∂L∂yi ∂yi∂xj\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_j}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}\,\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}∂xj​∂L​=i=1∑m​∂yi​∂L​∂xj​∂yi​​
    ∂L∂xj=∑i=1m∂L∂yi ∂yi∂xj\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_j}&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}\,\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}\end{aligned}∂xj​∂L​​=i=1∑m​∂yi​∂L​∂xj​∂yi​​​
    ∂L∂xj=∑i=1m∂L∂yi ∂yi∂xj\begin{aligned}&\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_j}\\&\quad =\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}\,\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}\end{aligned}​∂xj​∂L​=i=1∑m​∂yi​∂L​∂xj​∂yi​​​
    Why: Multivariable chain rule: xjx_jxj​ affects LLL through every yiy_iyi​; add over the paths (see the Calculus stop).
  2. =∑i(JT)ji (∇yL)i=(JT∇yL)j=\sum_{i}(J^{\mathsf T})_{ji}\,(\nabla_y L)_i=\big(J^{\mathsf T}\nabla_y L\big)_j=i∑​(JT)ji​(∇y​L)i​=(JT∇y​L)j​
    =∑i(JT)ji (∇yL)i=(JT∇yL)j\begin{aligned}&=\sum_{i}(J^{\mathsf T})_{ji}\,(\nabla_y L)_i\\&=\big(J^{\mathsf T}\nabla_y L\big)_j\end{aligned}​=i∑​(JT)ji​(∇y​L)i​=(JT∇y​L)j​​
    =∑i(JT)ji (∇yL)i=(JT∇yL)j\begin{aligned}&\\&\quad =\sum_{i}(J^{\mathsf T})_{ji}\,(\nabla_y L)_i\\&\quad =\big(J^{\mathsf T}\nabla_y L\big)_j\end{aligned}​=i∑​(JT)ji​(∇y​L)i​=(JT∇y​L)j​​
    Why: Jij=(JT)jiJ_{ij}=(J^{\mathsf T})_{ji}Jij​=(JT)ji​, and this is entry jjj of a matrix-vector product.

Q.E.D. ∎

✏️ A linear layer y=Wxy=Wxy=Wx

yi=∑kWikxky_i=\sum_k W_{ik}x_kyi​=∑k​Wik​xk​, so Jij=∂yi/∂xj=WijJ_{ij}=\partial y_i/\partial x_j=W_{ij}Jij​=∂yi​/∂xj​=Wij​, i.e. J=WJ=WJ=W:

∇xL=WT ∇yL,∂L∂Wij=∂L∂yi xj ⟹ ∇WL=(∇yL) xT\nabla_x L=W^{\mathsf T}\,\nabla_y L,\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{ij}}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}\,x_j\ \Longrightarrow\ \nabla_W L=(\nabla_y L)\,x^{\mathsf T}∇x​L=WT∇y​L,∂Wij​∂L​=∂yi​∂L​xj​ ⟹ ∇W​L=(∇y​L)xT
∇xL=WT ∇yL∂L∂Wij=∂L∂yi xj⟹ ∇WL=(∇yL) xT\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}\nabla_x L&=W^{\mathsf T}\,\nabla_y L\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{ij}}&=\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}\,x_j\\&\Longrightarrow\ \nabla_W L\\&=(\nabla_y L)\,x^{\mathsf T}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}∇x​L​=WT∇y​L​∂Wij​∂L​​=∂yi​∂L​xj​⟹ ∇W​L=(∇y​L)xT​​
∇xL=WT ∇yL∂L∂Wij=∂L∂yi xj⟹ ∇WL=(∇yL) xT\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}&\nabla_x L\\&\quad =W^{\mathsf T}\,\nabla_y L\end{aligned}\\\begin{aligned}&\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{ij}}\\&\quad =\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}\,x_j\\&\quad \Longrightarrow\ \nabla_W L\\&\quad =(\nabla_y L)\,x^{\mathsf T}\end{aligned}\end{gathered}​∇x​L=WT∇y​L​​∂Wij​∂L​=∂yi​∂L​xj​⟹ ∇W​L=(∇y​L)xT​​

The reason for the second formula: WijW_{ij}Wij​ appears only in yiy_iyi​, with ∂yi/∂Wij=xj\partial y_i/\partial W_{ij}=x_j∂yi​/∂Wij​=xj​. These two lines are all of Backprop for a linear layer; the full multi-layer derivation is in the Derivations stop.
